bib.title: Double-Dipping in the Data (Chapter 6, Statistics Done Wrong)

question: How does reusing data for both selection and testing, selecting extreme subjects, and stopping trials early bias results towards false positives and exaggerated effects?

results.claim: Stopped medical trials exaggerate effects by an average of 29% over similar trials not stopped early.
results.setup: Medical trials stopped early versus similar trials not stopped; footnote 7 not in extracted text
results.quote:
stopped medical trials exaggerate effects
by an average of 29% over similar studies that are not stopped
early

results.claim: Circular-analysis (double-dipping) rules are violated in neuroimaging literature perhaps as much as 40% of the time.
results.setup: Neuroimaging literature; source footnote 2 not in extracted text
results.quote: perhaps as much as 40% of the time

results.claim: Selecting regions by a screening test then testing the same data finds a nonexistent difference several times more often than the test's false positive rate suggests.
results.setup: Contrived fMRI walrus vs penguin example; no number given
results.quote: We will detect this nonexistent difference several times more often

results.claim: Peeking at a significance test after every added pair (start 10, plan 100 per group) with no true effect eventually dips below p=0.05, so stopping early gives a false positive.
results.setup: Simulation in Fig 6-1, no real difference between groups

We plan to use 100 patients in each group, but we start with

limits: Popular-science chapter: no original experiments; cited figures (29%, 40%) have footnote sources that are not in the extracted text.
Examples (monkey electrodes, walrus/penguin fMRI, Fixitol) are contrived or illustrative; no code or formulas given.
Tips are brief and do not give procedures for sequential analysis or selective inference.
practices: If you use your data to decide on your analysis procedure, use separate data to perform the analysis (Tips, p.71).
Split the dataset: choose regions of interest on one half and do the in-depth analysis on the other, at a cost in power (p.66).
Choose regions of interest by a criterion independent of the tested contrast, e.g. prior anatomical knowledge (p.66).
Confirm exploratory findings on a new, independent, sufficiently powered dataset (p.64).
To estimate a treatment effect when subjects were picked for being extreme, randomly split them into treatment and control groups (p.68).
Plan stopping rules in advance and adjust for multiple comparisons; use sequential analysis methods or stricter thresholds (p.70-71).
Register protocols and preselect a few evaluation points rather than testing after every observation (p.70).

terms.definition: using the same data twice: to select hypotheses or units and then to test them, so the test sees only the lucky ones
the observation that luck doesn't last forever: units selected for extreme values tend to be closer to average when measured again
a rule allowing investigators to end a study early if it is clear the experimental drug has a substantial effect
field that solves the p-value problem of variable group size by a stricter p threshold accounting for multiple testing, or different tests
exaggerated effect sizes arising because only the luckiest results pass the significance filter
